Neither — and the premise is the thing to fix first. More agents isn't a free upgrade: each extra agent is another model call, so it costs more and runs slower, and agents that split up a task can duplicate work or disagree about who's handling what. "More agents" has a real tax, not just a benefit.

Think about what your assistant actually does: answer from a manual, check a calendar, book a slot. That's three **tools**, not three agents. One agent with three tools, looping until it has an answer or a booking confirmed, can do all of that in a handful of calls. Splitting it into five or ten agents would mean, say, a "manual agent" handing off to a "calendar agent" handing off to a "booking agent" — each one a separate model call, each one needing the context explained to it again, for a task that one agent could just... do.

Multiple agents earn their cost when the subtasks are genuinely independent and can run in parallel (nothing here needs that — a booking request is one sequential chain: look up the rule, check the slot, book it), or when cramming everything into one agent's instructions and tools would overload it. A few tools on one focused assistant doesn't hit that wall.

So for your design review: start with one agent and three tools, and be ready to defend *that* as the simpler, cheaper choice — "why would you pay for ten model calls when one agent making three tool calls does the same job" is a stronger argument than picking a number of agents up front.

This is a bit ahead of where we'd planned to go next (context and memory come first in your mission), but it's worth its own real lesson once that's in place — multi-agent systems versus a single agent with tools is exactly the kind of judgment call your mission asks you to be able to defend. Want that as the next lesson, or finish context/memory first?

One quick check now: in your own words, why does splitting a task across agents cost more than giving one agent more tools?
